title: Winter animals
hookLine: owls, foxes and a hare in winter (Walden 15)

cards: Deep snow, the pond frozen hard, the woods gray and still. From a distance, a winter like that looks like a world switched off. Then the night begins to talk.
An owl calls from the trees. Out on the snow, foxes bark at each other in the dark. Before dawn, a red squirrel scrambles over the roof.
In the morning there are tracks everywhere, a whole night's traffic written down in the snow.

teach.b: In Winter Animals, Thoreau lies awake listening: the owl's call through the trees, geese passing over in the dark, the pond's ice groaning and booming as it shifts, and foxes out on the snow, barking in the night as if they were half dogs, half something wilder.
Winter wasn't silent. He just had to be still enough to hear it. Second, the corn.
He throws ears of sweet corn on the snow near his door and watches who comes. Red squirrels, dashing and stopping and dashing again, as if every move were a performance. Jays, loud and bold.
Chickadees in little flocks, so tame that one came close enough to land on the wood in his arms.
Once, he says, a sparrow lit on his shoulder for a moment, and he felt more honored by that than by any badge he could have worn. Third, the hare.
One evening a hare sits by his door, two paces from him, trembling, thin, ragged-eared, a poor small thing in a hard season.
Then it bounds away over the snow, stretching its body and legs to their full length, and suddenly it's all wild strength and freedom. Fourth, what this does. The cold season looks like an absence.
Thoreau shows it's a different kind of presence: fewer sounds, so each one carries; fewer leaves, so you can see who's moving. Winter didn't take the life away.
It made the life easier to notice.

how: Readers of Winter Animals often take from it a habit of patient watching in quiet seasons and places, noticing the life that remains when things look bare.

o: the animals that sleep through the cold months
the life Thoreau found around his cabin in the cold
the wild game Thoreau hunted to last the season

games.q: inside winter animals: tap the pairs.

s: Thoreau found the winter woods silent and empty
he heard owls, geese, booming ice and barking foxes.
Thoreau put out corn on the snow and watched who came
red squirrels, jays and chickadees came for it.
the hare by his door ran off in a panic and was never seen again
Thoreau describes it bounding away over the snow, all stretched-out strength and freedom.

games.q: it's deep winter at your cabin, and the woods look dead. what does Thoreau do?
o: stay inside and wait for spring.
throw corn out on the snow and watch who comes.
move to town until the thaw.
games.why: he put out sweet corn and watched squirrels, jays and chickadees arrive, and listened at night to owls, foxes and the ice.

practice: Whatever the season, find a place around you that seems empty, a bare window, a quiet street, a gray corner of the sky, and watch it the way Thoreau watched the snow by his door.
Wait for something to move: a bird crossing, a leaf, a cloud, a sound you hadn't heard. Each time, let it register: there's life here too.

wordCard.voice: Winter animals. Thoreau's frozen season full of owls, foxes, squirrels, chickadees and one trembling hare. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: winter life. A week of Walden, from the village to the cellar holes, ends in the snow. See you tomorrow.
